q: Do I need experience to start mountaineering?
a: No. Many people begin with trekking peaks and a beginner course. Technical climbs on snow, ice or rock need training first, so start with a course that teaches rope work, navigation and basic safety.

q: How fit do I need to be?
a: Good endurance and leg strength matter most. Train for several months before a trip, including long hikes with a loaded pack, and build up gradually.

q: What is the difference between trekking and mountaineering?
a: Trekking follows trails and usually needs no technical gear. Mountaineering involves snow, ice or rock and uses equipment such as ropes, crampons and ice axes.
For technical or high-altitude routes, a qualified guide is strongly recommended. Guides bring local knowledge, route-finding skills and safety training.

It depends on the route, but most trips need warm layers, a waterproof shell, sturdy boots, gloves, a headlamp, sun protection and a first-aid kit. Technical climbs also need a helmet, harness, ropes and crampons.

q: What is altitude sickness and how can I avoid it?
a: At high altitude there is less oxygen, which can cause headache, nausea and dizziness. Climb gradually, take rest days, drink enough water, and descend if symptoms get worse. Severe symptoms are an emergency. This is general information, not medical advice.
It is the process of your body adjusting to less oxygen. Climbers usually climb high during the day and sleep lower, adding rest days as they go up.

q: When is the best season to climb?
a: It depends on the region. The Himalaya is busiest before the monsoon in spring and again in autumn, the Karakoram in Pakistan has its main climbing season in summer, and the Alps are most popular in summer.
Yes, it carries real risks such as avalanches, weather changes and altitude illness. Training, careful planning, checking conditions and being willing to turn back greatly reduce them.
